extracted.intended_audience: public relations and journalism educators; curriculum committees; public relations program directors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, teaching, and assessing a university-level course in Writing for Public Relations, and for judging students' PR writing experience (including press releases and broadcast copy). Emphasizes specific writing experiences, quantity expectations, course structure, and pedagogical techniques (peer review, client review, publication incentives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics of preparing a press release for print
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed in Table I as a common writing experience for public relations students: 'Mechanics of preparing a press release for print.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty benchmarks (sample): desired goal coded 4.00 (6 to 10 experiences), minimum expectation coded 3.00 (3 to 5 experiences); faculty estimate of seniors ~2.50 (less than 3 experiences); PR senior self-report ~2.70 (less than 3). 51% of students had not prepared more than two press releases; 73% of seniors were below faculty minimum in this category (per sample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting material to particular media style
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapting material to particular media style (newspapers, specialized magazines, broadcasting, etc.) is a common PR writing experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course practice: tailor the same facts for different audiences/media (e.g., business page, alumni magazine, letter to television station suggesting picture/interview possibilities). Lesson emphasized: don't send a single all-purpose release; write versions for each audience and medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics for preparing radio news items
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics of preparing radio news items (radio news items prepared) identified as a writing type students should experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty benchmarks (sample): desired goal coded 3.63 (more than 5 experiences), minimum expectation 2.50 (less than 3); faculty estimate of seniors 1.83 (less than 1); PR senior self-report 1.78 (less than 1). 60% of students had never produced a radio news item; large shortfall compared with faculty expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics for preparing radio public service announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics for preparing radio public service announcements (radio public service items originated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty benchmarks (sample): desired goal coded 3.63 (more than 5), minimum 2.75 (less than 3); faculty estimate 2.38 (1 to 2 experiences); PR senior self-report 2.33 (1 to 2). Broadcast experience is generally low in print-oriented curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyzing timing of releases to maximize impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing timing of releases to maximize their impact or to meet specific communication objectives is a named learning objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should learn to plan release timing as part of communications objectives and campaign strategy; timing analysis is taught as a distinct skill in the course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics for preparing television news items
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics of preparing television news items (television news items originated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty benchmarks (sample): desired goal coded 3.38 (3 to 5 experiences), minimum expectation ~2.00 (1 or 2 experiences); faculty estimate of seniors and PR self-reports clustered at 'no experience' (faculty estimate ~1.0; PR self-report ~1.15). 91% of students had never prepared a television news item; broadcast training is a major deficit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics for preparing television public service announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics of preparing television public service items (PSAs) originated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty benchmarks (sample): desired goal coded 3.50, minimum expectation 2.00 (1 or 2 experiences); faculty estimate of seniors ~1.25 (no experience); PR senior self-report ~1.40 (no experience). 73% of seniors below minimum expectation in TV PSA preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing communication objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing communication objectives is identified as a common experience necessary for PR students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must learn to state client informational goals and craft copy to serve those objectives rather than maximize news conflict; this is part of converting PR principles into 'words-on-paper realities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyzing relationship between public relations practitioner and news media practitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing the relationship between the public relations practitioner and news media practitioner is a curricular objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course emphasizes the 'irony' and tensions in PR–newsroom relations (news seeks to magnify conflict; PR often works to mitigate conflict). Assignments discuss ethics, press relations strategies, and how to present material acceptable to newsrooms while serving client goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyzing problem situations and handling copy to mitigate conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing problem situations, including the handling of copy to mitigate conflict rather than to heighten it, is a stated objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction focuses on conflict-resolution roles of PR; students must balance truth/ethics with persuasion and avoid deliberate cover-up while minimizing exacerbation of controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing copy with a client/source prior to submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing copy with a client source prior to submission for publication (client copy review) is highlighted as a PR practice differing from journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course requires that any assignment produced for delivery to media be checked by the client (student's copy must carry client's initials). Guidance explains that this practice improves factual accuracy and that students careless with facts will face instructional consequences. Emphasizes client-review as standard PR workflow and ethical consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing a speech for delivery by another
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparing a speech for delivery by another person is listed among writing experiences (less likely in some programs but part of the 12 writing types).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty benchmarks (sample): desired goal coded 3.00 (3 to 5), minimum 2.75 (less than 3); faculty estimate 1.75 (less than 1); PR senior self-report 3.20 (3 to 5). In this sample, students sometimes exceeded faculty expectations in speech writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing business letters and memos to management
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing business letters and memos to management (e.g., interview preparation, negative news, publicity opportunity, ethical responsibilities) is a category of expected experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business letters: faculty desired goal ~3.25 (3 to 5), faculty estimate 2.25, PR senior self-report 4.13 (6 to 10). Memos to management are specifically called out as important for conveying internal PR thinking (interview prep, ethical responsibilities). These forms often show stronger student performance than broadcast items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing fact sheets
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparing fact sheets is one of the 12 identified writing assignment types for PR students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty benchmarks indicated a desired goal around the '3' code (3 to 5); faculty estimate of seniors often near 'no experience' (1.25); PR senior self-report mostly '1 or 2' experiences. Many students lacked sufficient fact-sheet preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing letters to the editor explaining client position
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing letters to the editor to explain a client position is included among expected PR writing tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty desired goal ~2.75 (less than 3), minimum expectation ~1–2; faculty estimate often 'no experience'; PR senior self-report ~1.66 (less than 1). High percentages (e.g., 85%) of seniors fell below minimum in this area in the sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other PR writings (brochures, ads, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other forms of writing such as brochures, ads, and other promotional materials are identified as part of PR training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty desired goal ~3.88 (less than 6 experiences), minimum ~3.00 (3 to 5); faculty estimate of seniors ~2.12 (1 or 2); PR senior self-report ~1.66 (less than 1). These applied/marketing forms are often underrepresented in students' experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-level faculty expectation framework and student self-report coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty used three levels—'Desired Expectation', 'Minimum Expectation', and 'Typical Achievement'—to evaluate student attainment; student responses used a numeric frequency code (1 to 5) to indicate number of experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric coding used by the study: (1) none; (2) 1 or 2; (3) 3 to 5; (4) 6 to 10; (5) more than 10. Faculty computed mean coded scores for desired/minimum/typical; compared with PR senior self-reports to identify gaps. Use this framework for benchmarking and assessing whether student experience meets program expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course content: valuing information and handling controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: One primary course goal: give students practical application in valuing information from a public relations perspective and teach how to handle controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction integrates traditional news values with client informational goals; students learn which information helps client goals, what editors will accept, and how to frame facts to solve problems rather than intensify conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course design: emphasis on laboratory assignments, broadcast practice, and publication incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Course structure described: approximately 25 writing assignments (about half under laboratory conditions), several broadcast assignments, peer and client review, extra credit for published stories, and no final examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course can more than double writing output of a typical senior. Policies: students must have client initials on media-deliverable assignments; peer review includes ranking and analytic write-ups used in grading; students encouraged to use exam week to produce additional publishable assignments for extra credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy review by peers (peer evaluation method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement peer review where students anonymously rank classmate releases and submit analyses explaining rankings; grades are based on rankings and quality of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: all students interview same source, produce a release, copies are photocopied and redistributed anonymously, students select top three and bottom three with explanations. This multi-day exercise assesses both writing effectiveness and critical perception; instructors grade on rankings and analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum sequencing and prerequisites for PR writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended prerequisites and sequencing: Writing for Public Relations is advanced and follows Writing for Mass Communications, Newswriting I, and Introduction to Public Relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program policy at the case institution: Newswriting I is required; Writing for Public Relations was paired as a required option with Magazine and Feature Writing; constraints include limiting required professional courses to about one-fourth of overall curriculum and preserving elective choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of background needed for PR practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: PR practitioners require a background beyond newswriting including editing, graphics, planning, campaigning, special events, public opinion, and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curriculum design should ensure students gain skills across these areas; PR writing cannot be isolated from campaign planning and media relations competencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program assessment recommendation: survey students' writing experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Many educators lacked precise knowledge of their students' writing experiences; the author recommends surveying student achievement as a basis for curriculum decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured questionnaires (faculty and student self-reports) to compare desired/minimum expectations with typical achievement; identify gaps (especially in broadcast) and adjust course offerings or prerequisites accordingly.
